title: Dynamic reservation failure mode case study
content:
Summary:
- This doc captures a root-cause investigation into a customer-facing OOM pattern seen in multi-tenant dedicated pools. Symptoms happened under mixed short-chat + long-completion workloads (seq len distribution: 32, 128, 1024). Not typical steady-state fragmentation — appears correlated with dynamic reservation adjustments + cross-stream free ordering.

Observed symptoms (high level):
- Intermittent OOMs on otherwise under-utilized GPUs (reported capacity 70% but 1GB free only when OOM occurred).
- Slow cudaMalloc stalls (~50-200ms spikes) preceding OOM; often followed by cascading perf regressions and request requeues.
- Heavier tail on allocation size distribution during canary rollout of model v2.

Repro and environment notes:
- Repro requires mixed traffic (concurrent short and long inferences) on the same CUDA device, with KV cache enabled and per-request workspace sizing set to heuristic=auto (legacy).
- Tested on NVIDIA A40 and A100; reproduces more reliably on A100 with larger total memory and aggressive caching.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 11.8; allocator: custom mempool + fallback to cudaMallocAsync -> cudaMalloc path.

Telemetry & traces collected:
- Per-request allocation timeline (telemetry id INF-1423): allocation bursts preceding OOM had 40% of allocations in the 4–16MB range, but the allocator was doing many small sub-allocs due to fragmentation.
- slow_cuda_alloc histogram: spike at 120ms and 180ms before OOM events.
- eviction logs: multiple cross-stream frees flagged as "delayed-free" (free recorded on the wrong stream then synced).
- slab-utilization sweep: nominal at 78% average, but hot-slab starvation observed (some slabs almost full, others nearly unused).

Allocator behaviour observations:
- MemPool reservation logic: on dynamic reservation shrink, mempool releases are batched and then requested back rapidly by concurrent requests — timing causes rapid free/alloc churn and small holes.
- cudaMallocAsync fallback triggers when mempool cannot satisfy an allocation. We observed calls entering cudaMallocAsync slow-path which serializes with the device allocator and produces visible stalls.
- Cross-stream deferred frees: several operators free tensors on compute streams and rely on stream callbacks; in high concurrency these callbacks execute out-of-order relative to other stream activity, leaving short-lived unreachable blocks that cannot be reused immediately.
- KV cache growth: kvcache uses pinned buffers and creates long-lived fragments that increase fragmentation pressure when combined with dynamic workspace allocations.

Key root-cause hypothesis (synthesized):
- Primary: Interaction between dynamic reservation adjustments + mempool batching leads to medium-sized internal fragmentation (4–32MB holes). During spikes of long requests, the runtime falls back to cudaMallocAsync for a few allocations; these serial slow-path allocations allow competing requests to run and create more holes, leading to competitive eviction and eventually a cudaMalloc call that fails (OOM) because the allocator can't find a contiguous region, despite total free memory existing.
- Secondary: Cross-stream deferred frees and non-coalesced pinned KV cache allocation patterns increase the fragmentation entropy, lowering probability of successful coalescing.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Replayed traffic with reservation disabled -> OOM did not reproduce.
- Forcing immediate frees (synchronous free on stream) reduced incidence by ~90% in experiment A (see results below).
- Changing mempool batch window from 200ms -> 20ms decreased fragmentation metric and eliminated bind-time cudaMallocAsync fallback.

Experiments run (short notes):
1) MemPool batch window tuning (PR 987):
   - 200ms (baseline): 6 OOMs/hour in stress test.
   - 50ms: 1 OOM/hour.
   - 20ms: 0 OOMs in 24h test.
   - CPU overhead: +3% on host CPU due to more frequent mempool ops.

2) Force synchronous frees for workspace allocations (temp patch):
   - Repros stopped for small-scale tests; not ideal for production (blocks progress).

3) KV cache compaction heuristic (off by default):
   - Aggressive compaction reduced fragmentation by ~8% but increased tail latency for long inferences (compaction pauses).

4) Preemptive guard allocation (alloc a small contiguous guard block at reservation time)
   - Reduced observed cudaMallocAsync slow-path by ~60% but increased resident usage by 1–2%.

Mitigations considered (tradeoffs):
- Short-term (canary): reduce mempool batch window to 20–50ms + enable guard allocation on heavy-tailed models. Pros: effective, low code changes. Cons: slight CPU and resident memory overhead.
- Medium-term: implement slab compaction pass during low-util windows (coalesce free segments). Pros: reduces fragmentation without raising resident memory. Cons: non-trivial complexity; requires safe concurrent compaction support.
- Long-term: build a cross-stream free-queue and ensure frees are visible to mempool earlier (move from stream callbacks to immediate host-visible release for workspace memory). Pros: addresses deferred-free issue. Cons: potential correctness/perf impacts if not carefully implemented.

Action items (owners):
- (Aisha) roll out mempool batch window change as canary to dedicated pools for models with mixed seq distribution (INF-1423). Target: next maintenance window.
- (Marcus) instrument cross-stream free events to emit "free-latency" telemetry and add a flag to force immediate host-visible free for workspace allocations (short-lived ramp). (PR: in review).
- (Elena) iterate on guard-allocation option and add feature flag per model. Run 72h soak.
- (Ravi) work with SRE to create an alert that correlates slow_cuda_alloc spikes + high slab-entropy metric.

Open questions / unresolved: 
- What is the right default for mempool batching across instance sizes? A40 vs A100 behaved slightly differently. Need quantitative knob mapping to device memory size.
- Could quantization or different memory alignment reduce fragmentation in practice? Need conv tests.
- Is there a light-weight compaction algorithm that is safe across streams without heavy synchronization?

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- Look into using cudaMemAddressFree or other low-level APIs to help coalesce on GPU side (if available across CUDA versions).
- Consider a background reclamation worker pinned to a CPU core that performs coalescing when device utilization < 40%.
- When enabling guard allocations, try adaptive guard size (proportional to recent allocation largest-req tail percentile).

Appendix: handy commands / traces to reproduce locally
- stress driver: infra/bench/stress_multi_tenant.sh --model=chat-mix --concurrency=48 --seq-dist="32:0.6,128:0.3,1024:0.1" --kv-cache=on
- capture heap timelines: PAYLOAD_ENABLE_HEAP_TRACE=1 ./serving-runtime --trace-allocs --trace-stream-frees > heap-trace.log
- quick check: python scripts/frag_summary.py heap-trace.log --window=1s

Links: INF ticket: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/INF-1423
PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987
Teardown note: after canary rollback, remember to disable guard flag to avoid resident bump.

Status: in_review — want feedback from SRE and applied-ml on canary rollout plan.

-- Aisha
